'''Patricia Jean Langhorne''' {{post-nominals|country=NZL|NZAM}} (born 1955) is a British–New Zealand [[Antarctic]] sea-ice researcher. She retired as a professor in the [[Department_of_Physics_at_the_University_of_Otago|Department of Physics]] at the [[University of Otago]], New Zealand, in 2020. She was previously head of department from 2012 to 2015. She was New Zealand's leading sea-ice physicist. For a time she led the observational component of one of New Zealand's National Science Challenges – the Deep South.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/24-million-niwa-led-deep-south-challenge|title=$24 million for NIWA-led Deep South Challenge|website=The Beehive|access-date=2016-06-17}}</ref>

==Early life, education and family==
Langhorne was born in Scotland in 1955.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://natlib.govt.nz/records/22506474 |title=Langhorne, Patricia Jean, 1955– |website=National Library of New Zealand |access-date=21 March 2025}}</ref><ref name="ODT 2017">{{cite news |url=https://www.odt.co.nz/lifestyle/magazine/science-ice |title=Science on ice |first=Bruce |last=Munro |date=12 June 2017 |work=[[Otago Daily Times]] |access-date=21 March 2025}}</ref> Her early life was spent in [[Torrance, East Dunbartonshire|Torrance]], near [[Kirkintilloch]], and she completed her schooling at [[Kilsyth]] Academy.{{cn|date=March 2025}} She earned a degree in physics from the [[University of Aberdeen]].<ref name="ODT 2017"/> From there she moved to [[Clare Hall, Cambridge|Clare Hall]]<ref>[https://www.cambridge-colleges.co.uk/clare-hall/#google_vignette University of Cambridge website, ''Clare Hall'']</ref> at the [[University of Cambridge]], where she completed her [[PhD]] on crystal alignment in sea ice in 1982, under the supervision of [[Peter Wadhams]]. She then held a fellowship with [[Newnham College, Cambridge|Newnham College]].<ref name="NZMS Newsletter">{{cite news |url=https://nzmathsoc.org.nz/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/NZMSnews86_Dec2002.pdf |work=Newsletter of the New Zealand Mathematical Society |issue=86 |title=Vernon Squire |access-date=21 March 2025}}</ref> This was supported by Rolls-Royce, at the [[Whittle Laboratory]], Cambridge.

At Kirkintilloch in 1987, Langhorne married mathematician [[Vernon Squire]], who became professor of applied mathematics at the University of Otago in October that year.<ref name="NZMS Newsletter"/><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/record-results/174830519367dcc4063657e |title=Results for Patricia Langhorne |website=Scotland's People |access-date=21 March 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.otago.ac.nz/news/newsroom/physics-professor-pat-langhorne-ponders-retirement |website=University of Otago |title=Physics Professor Pat Langhorne ponders retirement |date=6 August 2020 |access-date=21 March 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.otago.ac.nz/news/newsroom/professor-vernon-squire-retires-after-32-years-at-otago |website=University of Otago |title=Professor Vernon Squire retires after 32 years at Otago |date=30 April 2019 |access-date=21 March 2025}}</ref>

==Career and impact==
In 1985, Langhorne was invited to take part in an Antarctic experiment which brought her to New Zealand for the first time. This resulted in collaboration on examining the strength of sea ice with [[Bill Robinson (scientist)|Bill Robinson]], Vernon Squire and [[Tim Haskell]].<ref>Squire, V.A., Robinson, W.H., Langhorne, P.J., and Haskell, T.G. (1988) Vehicles and aircraft on floating ice. Nature, London, 333:159-161. doi:10.1038/333159a0</ref> The work was published in Nature and underpinned the use of sea ice runways for large aircraft. Since 1988 her work has focused on teaching physics and researching sea ice physical processes at the University Otago.  Langhorne was Head of the [[Department_of_Physics_at_the_University_of_Otago|Department of Physics]] at the University of Otago from 2012-2015.  Her work has involved over 20 research visits to Antarctica, mostly to the Ross Sea region. She has published extensively on the mechanical properties of sea ice under cyclic loading and its break-up by ocean waves, on the accretion and properties of [[frazil ice]] beneath the [[McMurdo Ice Shelf|McMurdo]] fast ice, and other aspects of sea ice and ice shelves.<ref>[https://www.dpmc.govt.nz/honours/lists/ny2019-nzam  New Zealand Government website, Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet section, ''New Year Honours 2019 - Citations for the New Zealand Antarctic Medal'']</ref>

Langhorne has been involved in the organisation of international scientific associations including the [[International Glaciological Society]] (IGS) and the [[International Association for Hydro-Environment Engineering and Research]] (IAHR).

Her leadership in the area was recognised with her being awarded funding<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.stuff.co.nz/science/74631050/university-of-otago-professor-gets-19m-for-antarctica-research|title=$1.9m for Antarctic research|website=Stuff|access-date=2016-06-17}}</ref> to lead the field component of one of the New Zealand National Science challenges, the Deep South, seeking to determine high latitude climate impacts on New Zealand.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.listener.co.nz/current-affairs/climate-change-current-affairs/the-shape-of-the-future/|title=The shape of the future - New Zealand Listener|date=2015-11-26|website=New Zealand Listener|language=en-US|access-date=2016-06-17}}</ref>

==Honours==
[[File:Pat Langhorne NZAM presentation.jpg|thumb|right|Langhorne (left) in 2019, after being presented with the [[New Zealand Antarctic Medal]] by the governor-general, Dame [[Patsy Reddy]]]]
In 2017, Langhorne was selected as one of the [[Royal Society Te Apārangi]]'s "[[150 women in 150 words]]", a project celebrating the contributions of women to expanding knowledge in New Zealand.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Pat Langhorne|url=https://www.royalsociety.org.nz/150th-anniversary/150-women-in-150-words/1968-2017/pat-langorne/|access-date=2021-04-27|website=Royal Society Te Apārangi}}</ref> 

In the [[2019 New Year Honours (New Zealand)|2019 New Year Honours]], Langhorne was awarded the [[New Zealand Antarctic Medal]], for services to Antarctic science.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/business/news/article.cfm?c_id=3&objectid=12182010|title=2019 New Year Honours: The full list|date=31 December 2018|work=New Zealand Herald|access-date=31 December 2018}}</ref>
